Row.Text: The Duchy of Athens was a crusader state founded in 1205 and ruled by the Burgundian de la Roche family and then the Brienne family. In 1311 it was seized by the mercenaries of the Catalan Company.
The Second Bulgarian Empire, with its capital at Tarnovo, was in 1299 recovering from Mongol domination under Tsar Theodore Svetoslav. Tarnovo fell to the Ottomans in 1393.
Caffa was the Genoese trading colony in the Crimea, the hub of Genoa's Black Sea commerce in grain, furs and slaves. It remained in Genoese hands until the Ottomans took it in 1475.
The Candarids, also called the Isfendiyarids, ruled Kastamonu and later the Black Sea port of Sinop. Among the longest-lived of the Anatolian beyliks, they survived until the reign of Mehmed II.

The Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia ruled the plain around Adana and the Taurus passes from its capital at Sis. Its port of Ayas was one of the great markets of the Levant. An ally of the Mongols, it was conquered by the Mamluks in 1375.
After the fall of Acre in 1291 the Kingdom of Cyprus, ruled by the Lusignan dynasty, became the last outpost of the crusader states. Famagusta grew into one of the richest ports of the Mediterranean.

The Despotate of Epirus was a Greek state in the western Balkans founded after the Fourth Crusade. From its capital at Arta it competed with Nicaea, and later with the restored Byzantine Empire, for the legacy of Rome.

The medieval Kingdom of Georgia reached its golden age under Queen Tamar around 1200. By 1299 it was a vassal of the Ilkhanate, and its throne was contested between rival members of the Bagrationi dynasty.

The Germiyanids ruled a powerful frontier principality from Kutahya, the immediate neighbour of Osman's small beylik. Their court was a centre of early Anatolian Turkish literature. Much of their territory passed to the Ottomans through a marriage alliance in the late 14th century.

The Golden Horde, or Ulus of Jochi, was the Mongol khanate of the western steppe. From its capital Sarai on the lower Volga it collected tribute from the Russian principalities and controlled the northern branch of the Silk Road.
The Hafsid dynasty ruled Ifriqiya from Tunis between 1229 and 1574. Tunis became the leading city of the Maghreb, until it was drawn into the struggle between the Ottomans and Habsburg Spain.

The Karamanids were a Turkmen dynasty of south-central Anatolia, based at Larende (modern Karaman) and Ermenek. For two centuries they were the most persistent rivals of the Ottomans in Anatolia, and they held Konya for long periods. Their lands were finally annexed by the Ottomans in the second half of the 15th century.

Karesi was a coastal principality around Balikesir facing the Dardanelles. Its seasoned sailors and soldiers joined the Ottomans after Orhan annexed the beylik in the 1340s, and they helped carry the Ottoman state across the straits into Europe.

Makuria was a Christian kingdom of Nubia on the middle Nile with its capital at Old Dongola. For six centuries it resisted its northern neighbours, but by 1299 it was weakened by Mamluk interventions.
The Sharifs of Mecca were the guardians of the holy cities of Islam. In 1299 they ruled the Hejaz under the protection of the Mamluk sultans of Egypt; in 1517 that role passed to the Ottomans.

Mentese was a seafaring beylik in Caria in south-western Anatolia, with its seat at Milas and Becin. Its fleets raided the islands of the Aegean, bringing it into conflict with the Knights Hospitaller and Venice.
The Angevin Kingdom of Naples ruled southern Italy after losing Sicily in 1282. Its kings also claimed lands across the Adriatic in Albania and Greece.

The Rasulid sultans ruled Yemen from Ta'izz and Zabid between 1229 and 1454. Through the port of Aden they controlled the spice trade between India and the Red Sea, and their court patronised scholars, astronomers and agriculture.
After the Sicilian Vespers of 1282 the island of Sicily rejected Angevin rule and chose a king from the House of Aragon. In 1299 it was still at war with the Angevin Kingdom of Naples.

The Empire of Trebizond was a Byzantine successor state on the Black Sea coast, ruled by the Grand Komnenoi from 1204. Rich from the trade that passed from Tabriz to the sea, it outlived Constantinople by eight years and fell to Mehmed II in 1461.
The Zayyanid kingdom of Tlemcen controlled the central Maghreb and the trans-Saharan trade routes that ended at its gates. In 1299 Tlemcen was enduring a long siege by the Marinids of Fez.
Anatolia, 1299. Lead Osman Bey's frontier principality, or any of the great powers of the age, on a real map that stretches from Vienna to Arabia.

It is the year 1299. The Seljuk Sultanate of Rum has crumbled under Mongol rule, and a patchwork of Turkmen beyliks now covers Anatolia. In the north-west, on the very border of the Eastern Roman Empire, Osman Bey rules a small principality around Sögüt.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Constantinople is still the greatest city of the Christian world, though its empire has shrunk to a few provinces. The Ilkhans rule Persia and Iraq from Tabriz, the Mamluk sultans hold Egypt, Syria and the holy cities, and Venice commands the sea. Beyond the Danube, Hungary, Austria and Poland are rising.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]The great powers begin with the cities they held in 1299. The Ottoman Beylik begins with a single settler near Bursa. History is yours to write.
